new_statements.quote: El grupo de acento (palabra fonológica), compuesto de una a cinco sílabas, se marca por pausa posible y los siguientes patrones acentuales predecibles: Los monosílabos se acentúan, sin importar el tono [...]. En los polisílabos con tono constante (alto o bajo) todas las sílabas se acentúan [...]. En los polisílabos de tono desigual, el acento ocurre sobre cada sílaba con tono alto: /pátu/ ['pátù] 'coca' [...]. La sílaba con tono alto que está seguida de una sola sílaba V de tono bajo recibe acento primario (marcado [ˈˈ]) y cualquier otra sílaba acentuada es secundaria: /ú̶tía/ [...] 'abeja', /yúkúuruka/ [...] 'tambor'.
new_statements.translation: The accent group (phonological word), made up of one to five syllables, is marked by potential pause and by the following predictable accentual patterns: Monosyllables are stressed, regardless of tone [...]. In polysyllables with constant tone (high or low) all syllables are stressed [...]. In polysyllables of unequal tone, stress falls on every high-toned syllable: /pátu/ ['pátù] 'coca' [...]. The high-toned syllable that is followed by a single low-toned V syllable receives primary stress (marked [ˈˈ]) and any other stressed syllable is secondary: /ú̶tía/ 'bee', /yúkúuruka/ 'drum'.
new_statements.citation: Whisler, David & Janice Whisler. 1976. Fonología del tatuyo. In Viola G. Waterhouse (ed.), Sistemas fonológicos de idiomas colombianos, Tomo III, 113-122. Lomalinda (Meta): Instituto Lingüístico de Verano / Ministerio de Gobierno.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File check: (20 pp., SIL file 21843, PDF metadata title 'Fonologia del tatuyo', author 'Whisler, David and Janice Whisler', 'In Sistemas fonologicos de idiomas colombianos 3, 113-22'). I rendered PDF pp. 17-18 (printed pp. 119-120) to images and read them directly, and compared with the held scanned text (. lines 646-690). The quoted passage is on the page exactly as reported: p.119 sec. 4 'El tono' ('Hay dos tonos fonemicos. El alto se marca /'/ y el bajo no se marca... Se ha encontrado todos los patrones tonales contrastables en palabras de una, dos o tres silabas'), then sec. 5 'El grupo de acento': 'El grupo de acento (palabra fonologica), compuesto de una a cinco silabas, se marca por…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tatuyo is a two-tone language (high vs low, all patterns contrastive on 1-3-syllable words, sec. 4). Stress is not contrastive but predictable from tone within the phonological word: every high-toned syllable is stressed (in all-high or all-low words every syllable is stressed; monosyllables always stressed); primary stress goes to a high-toned syllable that is immediately followed by a single low-toned onsetless (V) syllable, all other stressed syllables being secondary. No positional (initial/penult/final) rule is given. Gómez-Imbert 2004-05 independently analyses Tatuyo as a classic register-tone system (H/L on the mora, four lexical patterns AA/AB/BA/BB on bimoraic roots) and gives no stress rule, noting that moraic weight lacks the role it has in accentual languages.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Explicit: apart from the primary-stressed syllable (H followed by a single low V syllable), 'cualquier otra sílaba acentuada es secundaria' - i.e. all other high-toned syllables (and all syllables of level-tone words) carry secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None framed as exceptions. The primary-vs-secondary distinction is only defined for the configuration H + single low V syllable; for other word shapes the authors give equal stress marks on all high-toned (or, in level-tone words, all) syllables. Monosyllables stressed irrespective of tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the 'grupo de acento (palabra fonológica)', 1-5 syllables, delimited by potential pause; examples are citation forms of nouns. Dialect: Pamia clan, upper Piraparaná (fieldwork 1969-70). Later primary work (Gómez-Imbert 2004-05, Amerindia 29/30, secs. 5-5.1) treats Tatuyo as tonal (TBU = mora) with no accent statement, consistent with reading stress here as an epiphenomenon of high tone.
new_statements.identity_note: Whisler & Whisler 1976 describe the speech of the Pamia clan at the headwaters of the Piraparaná (Vaupés), noting few dialect differences; this is Tatuyo proper (tatu1247, ISO tav). Gómez-Imbert 2004-05 likewise describes Piraparaná Tatuyo (TAT) alongside Barasana (bara1380); only the TAT passages were used here.

sources.note: Sec. 4 'El tono' (p.119): two phonemic tones (high marked, low unmarked), all tonal patterns contrast on 1-3-syllable words. Sec. 5 'El grupo de acento' (pp.119-120): stress is predictable from tone within the accent group (phonological word, 1-5 syllables): monosyllables stressed regardless of tone; level-tone polysyllables stress every syllable; mixed-tone polysyllables stress every high-toned syllable; a high-toned syllable followed by a single low-toned V syllable takes primary stress, all other stressed syllables secondary.

sources.citation: Gómez-Imbert, Elsa. 2004-2005. Fonología de dos idiomas tukano del Piraparaná: barasana y tatuyo. Amerindia 29/30: 43-80. Paris: CELIA/CNRS (open PDF at amerindia.cnrs.fr).
sources.note: No stress rule. Sec. 5-5.1 (pp.67-69): Tatuyo has 'un sistema tonal clásico' with two register tones (Alto/Bajo), TBU = mora, four contrasting tonal patterns AA/AB/BA/BB on bimoraic lexical entries (c. 50 minimal pairs; BB only in nouns), words may be all-L or all-H, grammatical tone marginal (segmental prefixes where Barasana has tonal ones). Sec. 2.1 (p.49): 'El peso moráico no tiene el impacto que suele tener en lenguas acentuales como el latín'. Treats TAT as tonal, contrasting it with Barasana's restricted tone/pitch-accent system.
